questions.question: How does the focus of KIP-1050 on transaction error handling differ from KIP-890 server-side defense's handling of fencing during the prepare state?
questions.gold_answer: KIP-1050 targets consistent client-facing error handling and messages for EoS (developer experience), while KIP-890 concerns server-side protocol logic, such as deferring fencing until the complete state and returning CONCURRENT_TRANSACTIONS.

answer.text:
The two KIPs work at different levels. KIP-890 is a server-side protocol change. KIP-1050 is a client-side change to how errors are classified and exposed.

KIP-890 (Server Side Defense) aims to prevent common causes of hanging transactions and make other general improvements to transactions. On fencing during the prepare state, the discussion is only partly captured in the sources. Artem describes the idea, attributed to Jun, of deferring the fencing decision until the transition into the complete state. While in the prepare state, the coordinator would just return CONCURRENT_TRANSACTIONS without checking the epoch. The next producer id would have to be remembered during prepare. In the complete state the coordinator then needs it to decide on fencing and to let the old producer in if the request is a retried commit or abort. An alternative is to not reply to the client until the complete state is written. That would affect pipelining and probably need a separate KIP. Part 2 of KIP-890 also bumps the epoch after every transaction.

KIP-1050 (Consistent error handling for Transactions) does not change fencing mechanics. It aims to improve error handling and messages for exactly-once semantics, and so improve developer experience. It does this by grouping the exceptions the producer and transaction APIs can throw into categories, such as retriable, abortable, application-recoverable and invalid-configuration, under new exception superclasses. Reviewers' questions concerned which exceptions are user-facing, whether the changes are backward compatible, and how it relates to the existing TransactionAbortableException from KIP-890.

The two connect at one point. KIP-890 makes INVALID_PID_MAPPING fatal to the producer, and that is consistent with KIP-1050's "application recoverable" category, where the producer needs to restart.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer covers every required fact. It describes KIP-1050 as client-facing error handling and messaging for exactly-once semantics, aimed at developer experience. It describes KIP-890 as server-side protocol logic that defers fencing until the complete state and returns CONCURRENT_TRANSACTIONS during prepare. Nothing in it contradicts the gold answer.

questions.question: In the KIP-1043 group administration discussion, why did Andrew Schofield argue ConsumerGroupDescribe specifically needs a new error code, unlike heartbeat RPCs?
questions.gold_answer: Because classic and modern consumer groups coexist, and the admin client falls back to DescribeGroups on GROUP_ID_NOT_FOUND from ConsumerGroupDescribe, so a distinct error code is needed.

answer.text: The sources do not support the premise. Nothing here has Andrew Schofield arguing that ConsumerGroupDescribe needs a new error code *unlike* the heartbeat RPCs. In his 2024-08-02 message he proposed a new error code (then called INVALID_GROUP_TYPE) for all four of ConsumerGroupDescribe, ShareGroupDescribe, ConsumerGroupHeartbeat and ShareGroupHeartbeat, so the heartbeat RPCs were included, not contrasted. He said the other consumer group RPCs, such as ListOffsets and TxnOffsetCommit, would keep GROUP_ID_NOT_FOUND. The motivation he gave was that describing a share group with kafka-consumer-groups.sh gave a misleading 'Consumer group does not exist' error. ConsumerGroupDescribe returns GROUP_ID_NOT_FOUND with an empty message, and the classic DescribeGroups RPC returns NONE and makes the group look like a Dead group, with no error message field to tell them apart. Adding an error message in the broker he called brittle. Later, Lucas Brutschy described the final design as adding the new error 'only of the Describe RPCs', and in October Andrew said the error was by then named INCONSISTENT_GROUP_TYPE. He preferred the separate code because you don't have to read the message to know what went wrong, but he offered to drop it in favor of GROUP_ID_NOT_FOUND if David Jacot still preferred that. The sources do not show a specific argument that treats ConsumerGroupDescribe differently from the heartbeat RPCs.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer rejects the premise. It does not give the gold reasoning that classic and modern consumer groups coexist and that the admin client falls back to DescribeGroups when ConsumerGroupDescribe returns GROUP_ID_NOT_FOUND. That fallback is why a distinct error code is needed, and the answer omits it.

questions.question: How does the role of object storage in KIP-1150 Diskless Topics differ from its role in KIP-405 tiered storage?
questions.gold_answer: KIP-1150 proposes object storage as the primary storage for diskless topics, whereas KIP-405 uses remote storage for historical data no longer held locally on brokers.

answer.text:
In KIP-405 tiered storage, object storage is cold storage for older data. A log segment becomes eligible for upload once it is older than local.retention.ms, and it is then removed from local storage. Active log segments are not uploaded, so followers still replicate them from the leader, which incurs cross-AZ transfer costs.

In KIP-1150 Diskless Topics, object storage is the primary storage for the topic's data. The original design wrote through to object storage and acknowledged produce requests only after the object storage upload finished. That means data does not have to go through normal Kafka replication, which saves cross-AZ costs. The cost is higher produce latency, which Henry Cai estimates at around 100ms. Colin McCabe notes that this design still keeps some metadata on local disks, so it is not truly diskless.

The revised KIP-1150 design (September 2025) moves closer to KIP-405. Diskless data can be moved into tiered storage through the KIP-405 interfaces, and long-lived data must be tiered. Consumers are served from local segments that act as caches. These segments don't need to be durably stored and can be rebuilt without contacting other replicas. Produces remain leaderless through the Batch Coordinator.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer states both required facts. KIP-1150 makes object storage the primary storage for diskless topic data, and KIP-405 uses it for older, historical data no longer kept locally. Nothing in the extra detail contradicts the gold answer.

questions.question: What do KIP-1040 and KIP-581 have in common?
questions.gold_answer: Both deal with null-value handling: KIP-581 lets optional null fields keep null instead of always being replaced by their default, and KIP-1040 improves handling of nullable values in the InsertField/ExtractField Connect transformations.

answer.text: KIP-1040 and KIP-581 are linked through the `replace.null.with.default` configuration property. KIP-581 introduced that property to JsonConverter, so users can choose whether null fields that have a default value are replaced with the default. KIP-1040 was created to improve how nullable values are handled in the InsertField/ExtractField transformations (later also covering other transformations such as MaskField and ValueToKey), and it was needed as a result of KIP-581. Both are Kafka Connect-related KIPs. Both also had Mickael Maison involved: he picked up and drove KIP-581, and KIP-1040 was created through his account and he voted +1 (binding) on it. Chris Egerton was involved in both as well, commenting on KIP-581's design and voting +1 (binding) on both. Luke Chen and Tom Bentley voted on KIP-581, but the sources show no such votes on KIP-1040, so they are not shared participants.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer covers both required facts. It says KIP-581 lets users choose whether null fields that have a default are replaced by that default, which matches keeping null instead of always substituting the default. It says KIP-1040 improves handling of nullable values in InsertField/ExtractField. The extra participant details do not contradict the gold answer.

questions.question: How does KIP-1194's handling of racks in replica assignment differ from the rack-aware anti-affinity support in KIP-1151's reassignment algorithm?
questions.gold_answer: KIP-1151 treats rack awareness as one goal alongside minimal movement and balancing, while KIP-1194 weights rack allocation by brokers per rack to balance load when racks are uneven.

answer.text: The sources only partly support a comparison. KIP-1194 (email:4544c7af7cafe477:0) proposes a replica assignment strategy that prioritizes balanced distribution across brokers while weighting rack-level allocation by the number of nodes per rack. It targets uneven rack configurations, where uneven broker counts per rack create bottlenecks, and it aims to keep rack awareness in place. In a later thread, peng describes it as a `WeightedReplicaPlacer`, an alternative to the current `StripedReplicaPlacer` (email:b20c1e9dc141ef41:0). KIP-1151 (email:c866517954b16e6c:0, email:93f368930f51cdba:0) is a replica reassignment algorithm. It lists "Anti-Affinity Support: Support rack-aware allocation when enabled" as one of its goals, alongside minimal movement, even replica balancing, leader balancing, and ISR order optimization. So at a high level, KIP-1194 is about initial replica placement and weights racks by broker count, while KIP-1151 is about reassignment and supports rack-aware allocation when enabled, with the goal of minimizing movement. The sources do not describe how KIP-1151's anti-affinity logic actually handles racks, for example whether it accounts for uneven rack sizes. They also give no detail on KIP-1194's algorithm beyond the summary. A precise technical comparison therefore cannot be made from these sources.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer says KIP-1151 treats rack-aware allocation as one goal among others, such as minimal movement and balancing. It also says KIP-1194 weights rack allocation by brokers per rack to handle uneven racks. These are both required facts, and nothing in the answer contradicts the gold.

questions.question: How do the proposed changes in KIP-1058 (transaction consumer load on remote storage) and KIP-1105 (remote log manager thread pools) differ in nature?
questions.gold_answer: KIP-1058 was narrowed to adding one backward-compatible field, txnIdxEmpty, to the RemoteLogSegmentMetadata event; KIP-1105 makes remote log manager thread-pool configs dynamically changeable.

answer.text: The two KIPs address different problems. KIP-1058 is a read-path performance optimization. When a consumer uses READ_COMMITTED, the broker may have to traverse many remote segments to collect aborted transactions, which puts pressure on remote storage. The KIP reduces this by adding one backward-compatible field (txnIdxEmpty, default false so old events are assumed to have a txn index) to the RemoteLogSegmentMetadata event. That lets the broker skip fetching transaction indexes for segments that have none. KIP-1105 is an operational and configuration change. It makes the remote log manager thread-pool configs dynamically updatable, so operators don't need a rolling restart to resize pools, and it adds graceful handling of remote-log components during server startup (an `isReady` API). It skips the deprecated remote.log.manager.thread.pool.size config and covers the copier and expiration pools. In short, KIP-1058 optimizes consumer fetch behavior and reduces load on remote storage, while KIP-1105 improves how the remote log manager's thread pools are managed and configured.

answer.text: Matthias objected because of the unclear history retention and the compatibility problem. (1) If the table isn't explicitly materialized, it is already materialized as a non-versioned store in the old program, so adding a grace period would require switching the store type. That would be a breaking change, potentially needing an application reset or the versioned-store upgrade path (KIP-914), plus a program change to materialize explicitly as versioned. (2) It was unclear what history retention would be picked for an implicitly materialized versioned table, which has a significant disk-usage impact. He also noted that the join might not materialize the actual join table, only an upstream table accessed via ValueGetter. He therefore proposed pushing the burden onto users: don't support non-versioned KTables, require explicit versioned materialization (directly or upstream), require history retention to be larger than the grace period, and treat adding a grace period as not backward compatible. questions.question: How does the focus of KIP-1137 on configuration precedence in tool scripts differ from KIP-1147's focus on command-line tool arguments?
questions.gold_answer: KIP-1137 standardizes configuration precedence and required-argument checking across tool scripts, while KIP-1147 aligns the names of command-line arguments across all Kafka command-line tools.

answer.text:
KIP-1137 is about configuration precedence: standardizing which source wins when the same setting is given in several places in Kafka tool scripts. Those places are a specific command-line argument, in-line properties on the command line (e.g. --producer-property), and a config file. Its discussion thread says it should give tool scripts more consistent behavior in configuration precedence and required-argument checking. For example, a script should check the command-line argument, in-line property, and config file (e.g. for --bootstrap-server) before declaring a run failed. Its proposed mergePropertiesWithPrecedence() would also warn when the same config appears in multiple sources. It began as KAFKA-10043 "Standardize Property Loading Priority", and Chia-Ping noted that changing precedence needs a KIP to follow the compatibility policy.

KIP-1147 is about consistency of the names of command-line arguments across all Kafka command-line tools. Examples include aligning --producer-props with --producer-property, adding --consumer-property to the consumer perf tools, replacing `messages` with `num-records`, adding reporting-interval, and aligning --config or --broker-list with --command-config or --bootstrap-server. It also adds --bootstrap-server to kafka-producer-perf-test.sh. Andrew said KIP-1147 does not change the precedence of configs for existing tools. He deferred completion of any precedence changes to KIP-1137 to keep the scope manageable. Tommi said KIP-1137 was fully aligned with the precedence described in KIP-1147.

In short, KIP-1147 standardizes what the arguments are called, while KIP-1137 standardizes which value takes priority when a setting is supplied through several routes.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer covers every required fact. It describes KIP-1137 as standardizing configuration precedence and required-argument checking in tool scripts, and KIP-1147 as aligning argument names across all Kafka command-line tools. questions.question: How do the stated goals of KIP-1023 (follower fetch from tiered offset) and KIP-1241 (delayed upload) differ in the tiered storage problem each addresses?
questions.gold_answer: KIP-1023 aims to cut broker rebalance/rebuild times by letting followers fetch from the tiered offset, while KIP-1241 aims to cut redundant storage by delaying upload of segments to remote storage.

answer.text: They pull in opposite directions on the tiered storage problem they address. KIP-1023 targets replica rebuild/bootstrap time. When a cluster has tiered storage enabled, a new or empty follower can skip replicating all the data already in remote storage. It starts from the tiered offset (last-tiered-offset / earliest-pending-upload offset), builds auxiliary state for the earlier data, and fetches only the tail. The aim is to significantly cut Kafka rebalance/rebuild times and the time a partition spends under-replicated. KIP-1241 targets storage redundancy and cost. Today Kafka uploads all non-active local segments to remote storage immediately, even while they are still within the local retention period, so the same data sits in both tiers. Delaying the upload avoids storing the duplicate copy during the local retention window, which wastes capacity and cost when no real-time remote-based consumption is needed. It would be an optional topic-level setting, not the default. The two also interact. Haiying Cai argued that uploading ASAP helps fast bootstrapping, which is what KIP-1023 solves, so delaying upload runs against that benefit. Jian replied that the feature is optional and suits topics with a low remote-to-local retention ratio.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer gives both required facts: KIP-1023 reduces rebalance/rebuild times by having followers fetch from the tiered offset, and KIP-1241 reduces redundant storage by delaying segment upload. Its extra detail does not contradict the gold answer.

questions.question: How do the problems addressed by KIP-923's grace period for stream-table joins and KIP-955's foreign-key stream-table join differ?
questions.gold_answer: KIP-923 adds a grace period that buffers stream records before joining (raising whether the table must be a versioned store), while KIP-955 joins each stream record to zero, one or many table records via a foreign-key field.

answer.text:
They address different problems in stream-table joins.

KIP-923 (Walker Carlson) is about ordering and timing semantics. It proposes adding a grace period and a buffer on the stream side of a stream-table join, so stream records are processed in timestamp order. This matches the recent improvements of versioned tables. Discussion centers on out-of-order vs. late records, how stream time advances, and interactions with the table's versioned store history retention. Records can get stuck in the buffer if stream time doesn't advance, and large timestamp gaps can cause join misses once history retention has elapsed. Other points are whether the table must be versioned and what happens when users change the grace period. It does not change which records join; the join is still a 1:1 enrichment of the stream by key.

KIP-955 (Igor Fomenko) is about the join key and cardinality. It proposes a new DSL API to join a stream to a table on a foreign key extracted from the table (right) side, without aggregation. One stream event can match many table rows (e.g., an order event joined to many order items) and emit multiple results. Aggregation could be added afterward as a separate step. Matthias Sax questioned whether this fits a stream-table join, which he sees as a 1:1 enrichment. He called the multi-record output a "flatMap" side-effect and suggested alternatives such as re-keying and aggregating the table on the join attribute. Igor argued this mirrors SQL join behavior and scales better.

In short, KIP-923 is about when and in what order records are joined (timestamp ordering via grace period and buffering), while KIP-955 is about what they are joined on (foreign key) and the resulting 1:n semantics.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer covers both required points. For KIP-923 it states that a grace period buffers stream records before the join and that discussion raised whether the table must be versioned. questions.question: Why did Lan Ding rename the configuration proposed in KIP-1196 that limits the size of group coordinator appends?
questions.gold_answer: The original name could be misleading.

answer.text: Lan Ding renamed the config from `group.coordinator.append.max.bytes` to `group.coordinator.append.max.buffer.size` because the original name was potentially ambiguous/misleading. It suggested a hard limit on message size. The setting actually controls only the buffer caching behavior (a soft limit): larger writes are still allowed up to the topic's `max.message.bytes`, and an oversized buffer is just not kept for reuse. Lan said the goal is to decouple the buffer size from the maximum allowed message size, so that the buffer is not cached for occasionally large messages. Lan confirmed this to Sean Quah, saying the original name "could indeed be misleading."

questions.judge_rationale: The gold answer requires one fact: the original name could be misleading. The system answer states exactly this and quotes Lan saying the name "could indeed be misleading." The extra detail it adds does not contradict the gold answer.

questions.question: Per KIP-952, what failure do users hit if they enable tiered storage right after upgrading from a Kafka version older than 2.8?
questions.gold_answer: NullPointerExceptions, because older segments lack producer snapshot files.

answer.text: Per KIP-952's motivation, versions older than 2.8 did not create producer snapshot files for segments. If a customer upgrades from <2.8 to 3.6 and enables tiered storage right away, segments that lack a producer snapshot file cause NullPointerExceptions (NPEs). To avoid this today, the customer must wait until all segments lacking snapshot files have expired and been deleted before enabling the feature. KIP-952 aims to fix this by regenerating segment-aligned producer snapshots on upgrade.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer gives both required facts: the failure is NullPointerExceptions, and the cause is that segments from versions before 2.8 have no producer snapshot files. The extra details do not contradict the gold answer.

questions.question: How does the purpose of KIP-1037's change to WriteTxnMarkers differ from that of KIP-1228's change to WriteTxnMarkersRequest?
questions.gold_answer: KIP-1037 changes authorization, letting WriteTxnMarkers work with Alter Cluster permission, whereas KIP-1228 changes the request contents by adding a transaction version to strengthen EOS guarantees.

answer.text: The two KIPs change WriteTxnMarkers for different reasons. KIP-1037 (2024) is about authorization. WriteTxnMarkers was originally an inter-broker API requiring ClusterAction on the Cluster resource. After KIP-664 let it be called externally from the AdminClient to abort a hanging transaction, KIP-1037 proposed allowing it with the Alter permission on the Cluster. That is more consistent with other admin actions such as CreateAcls and DeleteAcls. It was resolved as KAFKA-16513, fixed in 3.8.0. KIP-1228 (2025) is about the request's content and transaction semantics. It adds a transaction version (TV) to the WriteTxnMarkersRequest, per marker, so the epoch check can be tightened when epoch bumping at the end of every transaction is supported (TV2). Ritika Reddy described it as strengthening EOS guarantees, and it is linked to KAFKA-19446, 'TV2 late marker can violate EOS guarantees'. The discussion settled on an API version bump rather than a tagged field. In short, KIP-1037 changes who may call the API (permission model), while KIP-1228 changes what the request carries so the broker can enforce correct epoch validation for exactly-once semantics.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer covers both required facts. It says KIP-1037 is about authorization, allowing WriteTxnMarkers with the Alter permission on the Cluster. It says KIP-1228 adds a transaction version to WriteTxnMarkersRequest to strengthen EOS guarantees. Nothing in it contradicts the gold answer.

questions.question: In the KIP-1176 active log segment tiered storage discussion, which kernel setting did Jun Rao say applies to all dirty files, thereby affecting flush frequency for WAL-enabled topics?
questions.gold_answer: dirty_expire_centisecs

questions.question: In the KIP-910 discussion on emitting source offsets without records, what objection did Chris Egerton raise about adding the feature to Kafka Connect, given Debezium's existing behavior?

answer.text: In his 2023-03-28 review, Chris Egerton noted that the only use case identified so far (in the KIP and the KAFKA-3821 discussion) for emitting offsets without source records was CDC source connectors like Debezium. Debezium already supports this exact feature by emitting heartbeat records that carry offsets which can't be tied to regular source records. He therefore questioned why Kafka Connect should add the feature when the problem is already solved for the very small set of connectors that would need it, and asked for other practical use cases. On 2023-04-12 he reinforced this: the added cognitive load for connector developers and Connect administrators costs too much to justify by pointing to an already-solved problem encountered by a single group of connectors (Debezium). He said realistic cases where the feature would be useful, beyond ones already addressed or addressable with much simpler changes, had not been provided. He also found the file-based source connector example confusing.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer covers every required fact: Debezium already supports this via heartbeat records, the feature would solve an already-solved problem for the few CDC connectors that need it, and Egerton asked for other practical use cases. questions.question: How does the Kafka component targeted by KIP-1113's rack-aware assignor changes differ from the one targeted by KIP-1194's uneven-rack replica assignment?
questions.gold_answer: KIP-1113 changes client-side consumer partition assignors (leader-rack-aware), while KIP-1194 changes how replicas are assigned to brokers across racks with uneven node counts.

answer.text: KIP-1113 targets the client-side consumer partition assignor (the rack-aware assignor used with partition.assignment.strategy, building on KIP-881). It proposes new assignors, LeaderRackAwareCooperativeStickyAssignor and LeaderRackAwareRangeAssignor, which fetch only from leader replicas and use the leader's rack to balance partitions across consumers. This removes the need for the broker-side replica.selector.class setting. KIP-1194 targets the broker/cluster-side replica assignment, meaning where a topic's partition replicas are placed across brokers and racks. It proposes a strategy that balances load across brokers while weighting rack-level allocation by the number of nodes per rack, to handle uneven broker distribution across racks. In short, KIP-1113 concerns how consumers are assigned partitions, and KIP-1194 concerns how replicas are assigned to brokers.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer gives both required facts. KIP-1113 targets client-side consumer partition assignors that are leader-rack-aware, and KIP-1194 targets replica-to-broker assignment across racks with uneven node counts. Nothing in it contradicts the gold answer.

questions.question: In the KIP-1042 wildcard-ACL vote thread, a ticket was proposed as a faster ACL store without the KIP's wildcards; how does it quickly locate candidate ACLs?
questions.gold_answer: It splits ACLs into groups by similarity of resource name and moves through a trie keyed on the resource name to locate candidates.

answer.text: The ticket is KAFKA-17423, which builds on KAFKA-17316 by creating a Trie implementation (without the new KIP-1042 wildcards) and is described as an order of magnitude faster at processing ACL requests. The Trie locates candidate ACLs by descending the trie along the resource name instead of repositioning within a sorted list of all ACLs via binary search. While descending: (1) a matching DENY stops the search, since it overrides anything lower; (2) only LITERAL matches are looked for, and reaching a matching resource name or a leaf means there are no LITERAL matches. If there is no DENY or LITERAL match, it walks back up the same path checking the nodes already visited for a PREFIX match, so it doesn't have to search again. Claude Warren believes points 1 and 2 account for much of the speed increase, because they avoid binary-search repositioning in a sorted list of all ACLs.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer gets the trie part right: candidates are found by descending a trie along the resource name, which matches the gold's 'moves through a trie keyed on the resource name'. It does not mention the other required fact, that ACLs are split into groups by similarity of resource name. Nothing in the answer contradicts the gold.

questions.question: How does the main problem addressed by KIP-1241's delayed segment upload differ from that of KIP-1248's direct consumer fetching from remote tiered storage?
questions.gold_answer: KIP-1241 targets redundant storage cost by delaying remote upload of segments still within local retention; KIP-1248 targets broker network and cache load from large backfill reads by letting consumers fetch remotely.

answer.text:
They address different problems in tiered storage.

KIP-1241 (Jian Fu) targets remote storage cost and redundancy. Kafka currently uploads non-active segments to remote storage immediately, even while they are still within the local retention period. The same data is therefore stored in both tiers, and the remote copy gives no immediate benefit because reads prioritize local data. KIP-1241 proposes a topic-level optional feature that delays the upload, so the duplicated copy is not kept in remote storage during the local retention window. Jian notes the savings depend on the local-to-remote retention ratio, for example 1 day local with 3-7 days remote, and that it does not change the default behavior.

KIP-1248 (Henry Haiying Cai) targets read-path performance and broker load. Today, when a new or fallen-off consumer needs older data that is no longer in local storage, the broker must download it from remote tiered storage and relay it to the consumer. KIP-1248 proposes letting consumers fetch directly from remote tiered storage. This avoids hitting the broker's network capacity and cache performance, and it is useful for serving large backfills.

The two are in tension on timing. KIP-1241 wants the remote copy to appear later, to save cost. Haiying Cai argues that uploading as early as possible helps fast bootstrapping of new brokers and consumer backfill reads, which KIP-1248 relies on.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer covers both required facts. It says KIP-1241 targets redundant remote storage cost by delaying upload of segments still within local retention. It says KIP-1248 targets broker network and cache load from backfill reads by letting consumers fetch directly from remote storage. Nothing in it contradicts the gold answer.

questions.question: In the KIP-977 discussion on partition-level throughput metrics, what overhead concern did Kirk True raise about leaving partition filtering to downstream metrics providers?
questions.gold_answer: Metric data would still have to be held in memory until it is flushed, so filtering at a lower layer would not avoid that memory overhead.

answer.text: Kirk True noted that if partition-level filtering were relegated to a lower layer (the downstream metrics providers/framework), Kafka would still have to store the metric data in memory until it is flushed. He asked whether that in-memory overhead would be a concern. He also questioned whether all heavily used metrics providers support dynamic filtering, since the approach is a greatest-common-denominator scenario.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer states the required point: filtering at a lower layer would still require holding metric data in memory until it is flushed, so that memory overhead remains. The extra point about whether providers support dynamic filtering doesn't contradict the gold answer.

questions.question: In the KIP-1090 flaky tests discussion, what did Chia-Ping Tsai suggest should be excluded from flaky test management and retries?
questions.gold_answer: Unit tests; only integration tests would be retried and annotated as flaky, via a new flag filtering the retry plugin.

answer.text: Chia-Ping Tsai suggested that unit tests should be excluded from flaky test management and retries. Specifically: (1) unit tests cannot carry an "@Flaky" annotation if annotations are used for flaky management, and (2) CI should enable retry only for integration tests, which could be done by adding a flag such as "allowRetryUnitTest" and a filter in the retry plugin. He summarized the rule as "unit test should always be deterministic (non-retryable)", arguing that allowing tests to be marked flaky in a module like raft, which has no integration tests, would be dangerous to protocol correctness and metadata consistency. David Arthur agreed with this rule and suggested auto-failing a test marked "flaky" that is not also tagged "integration".

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer names unit tests as the exclusion and says only integration tests would be retried and annotated, via a new flag and a filter in the retry plugin. That covers every required fact, and the extra details do not contradict the gold answer.

questions.question: How do the tiered storage problems addressed by KIP-852 and KIP-952 differ in focus?
questions.gold_answer: KIP-852 concerns efficiently calculating remote log size, while KIP-952 concerns missing producer snapshots (causing NPEs) when enabling tiered storage after upgrading from versions before 2.8.

answer.text:
KIP-852 is about performance and availability of tiered storage operations. It adds an API, remoteLogSize, so the size of the log in the remote tier can be obtained without a full scan. Today the only option is listing all remote segment metadata through listRemoteLogSegments() and aggregating it. That is slow when num_remote_segments is large and when the RemoteLogMetadataManager's underlying storage is slow. It can cause bursts of full-scan requests when several leadership failovers happen at once, and it delays the start of archival, which can leave data building up locally and fill the disk. The KIP also adds a metric, and it was accepted on 2023-07-18.

KIP-952 is about upgrade compatibility. A cluster upgraded from Kafka versions older than 2.8 has log segments with no producer snapshot files. A customer who enables tiered storage after upgrading to 3.6 would hit NPEs unless every segment lacking a snapshot has already expired and been deleted. KIP-952 proposes regenerating segment-aligned producer snapshots when upgrading to a version that supports tiered storage. Its author argued it might block 3.6.0, but Satish Duggana said he did not think it was a blocker, and it remained under discussion.

In short, KIP-852 optimizes how remote log size is calculated, while KIP-952 fixes enabling tiered storage on topics created before version 2.8.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer covers both required facts. It says KIP-852 is about efficiently calculating remote log size. It says KIP-952 addresses missing producer snapshots that cause NPEs when tiered storage is enabled after upgrading from versions before 2.8. Nothing in it contradicts the gold answer.

questions.question: Do Kafka Streams KIP-904 (subtractor/adder ordering) and KIP-914 (versioned store join semantics) change the same kind of processor?
questions.gold_answer: No. KIP-904 concerns the order in which an aggregation's subtractor and adder are called, while KIP-914 concerns stream-table and table-table join semantics for versioned stores.

answer.text: Only partly. KIP-914 was proposed to update the stream-table and table-table join processors for versioned stores. During implementation it was extended to the table filter processor and to table aggregations over versioned tables. KIP-904 is about the subtractor being called before the adder if the key has not changed, which is table-aggregation behavior. The sources describe it only through its title and through discussion of the repartition topic's "Changed" serde format and groupBy key equality. The two KIPs therefore overlap on table aggregation and on the repartition topic format. KIP-904 changed that format in 3.5, and KIP-914 first planned to add a timestamp to it but later dropped that change. Beyond that they are different: KIP-904 is not about versioned stores or join semantics, and KIP-914 is not about subtractor/adder ordering. The sources do not spell out KIP-904's full scope, so this comparison is based on its title and the discussion snippets.

questions.judge_rationale: The gold answer says plainly that the two KIPs do not change the same kind of processor: KIP-904 concerns aggregation subtractor/adder ordering and KIP-914 concerns join semantics for versioned stores. The system opens with "Only partly" and claims the KIPs overlap on table aggregation, which contradicts the gold's "No". It does correctly describe what each KIP is about.

questions.question: What differing goals motivate KIP-1188's new Connect client override policy and KIP-935's extension of AlterConfigPolicy with existing configurations?
questions.gold_answer: KIP-1188 aims to make Connect more secure by default by allowing only selected client config overrides, while KIP-935 aims to enable more complex alter-config policies by exposing existing configurations.

answer.text:
The two KIPs are driven by different goals.

KIP-1188 (Mickael Maison) is about security and safe defaults in Kafka Connect. It adds a new ConnectorClientConfigOverridePolicy implementation with an allowlist, so users can selectively allow specific client configuration overrides. Maison said this would help address the several security issues that have affected Connect and make Connect more secure by default. The default allowlist is empty, so users must list every configuration they want to allow. The KIP is planned to become the default policy in Kafka 5.0. Maison also said PrincipalConnectorClientConfigOverridePolicy could be deprecated, because it has been a source of security issues and does not support the newer SASL configs. Luke Chen's reply, "to make Kafka safer", fits this framing.

KIP-935 (Jorge Esteban Quilcate Otoya) is about the expressiveness of broker/topic config policies. It extends AlterConfigPolicy with the existing configurations so that more complex policies can be written. Today a policy cannot compare a requested change against the current configs. The KIP says earlier related KIPs had been abandoned, and its scope is narrower than theirs. Christo Lolov backed it because of the configuration dependencies he runs into often. The discussion also showed that the policy's "requested configs" mean different things in the legacy and incremental alter-config APIs, and that some deletions are mishandled (KAFKA-14195). Because of this, the design moved toward a new API that receives both old and new config maps (AlterConfigV2Policy).

In short, KIP-1188 restricts which Connect client overrides are allowed, in order to harden security. KIP-935 gives AlterConfigPolicy richer context, namely the existing configs, so that operators can enforce more sophisticated config-change rules.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer gives both required facts. KIP-1188 makes Connect more secure by default by allowing only selected client config overrides through an allowlist. KIP-935 exposes existing configurations so that more complex alter-config policies can be written. Nothing in it contradicts the gold answer.

questions.question: In the KIP-969 discussion on range interactive queries for versioned state stores, what did Bruno Cadonna suggest about how range queries should be structured?
questions.gold_answer: Split range queries into two classes: one returning a single version of keys in the range, and one returning multiple versions, to reduce meaningless combinations.

answer.text: Bruno Cadonna proposed splitting range queries for versioned state stores into two query classes, mirroring the split for single-key queries. One class would return a single version of the keys in a range (the latest or an "as of" version), and the other would return multiple versions of the keys in a range over a time range. He argued this reduces meaningless combinations and avoids edge cases such as specifying a time range together with latest() or asOf() on a key range (e.g., ambiguity in `fromTime(t1).latest().toTime(t2)`: is it [t1, t2] or [-INF, t2]?). He suggested both classes could be proposed in the KIP, and as an alternative, keeping one class with a "last call wins" rule. Later, he said that using TimestampedRangeQuery to query the latest versions was totally fine, and that users could report problems and more could be added then. He also questioned whether orderByKey()/orderByTimestamp() were needed given withAscendingKeys() etc., and asked to agree on naming (withAllKeys() preferred) across KIP-969, KIP-997 and RangeQuery.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer includes every required fact. It describes splitting range queries into two classes, one returning a single version of keys in the range and one returning multiple versions, and gives the stated aim of reducing meaningless combinations. The extra details it adds do not contradict the gold answer.

questions.question: In KIP-932 (Queues for Kafka), why are share group partition assignments not persisted, unlike consumer group assignments?
questions.gold_answer: Assignments surviving a group coordinator change matters little, since partitions needn't be safely transferred between members as in consumer groups, so persisting is an unnecessary optimisation.

answer.text: Originally, KIP-932 deliberately did not persist share group assignments, but that decision was later reversed. The original reasoning (April 2024) was that it matters much less if assignments survive a group coordinator change. Share groups have no need to safely transfer partitions from member to member the way consumer groups do. So not persisting them was an optimisation; Andrew said persisting "wouldn't do any harm, but it just seems unnecessary." He also said the share group does not persist the target assignment, and in May 2024 he was "not inclined to persist the assignments in this KIP," though persisting them to smooth assignment after a GC change would be an easy enhancement. However, per the 2024-08-13 update, this is no longer true. During implementation, not persisting assignments made it hard to fit the coordinator framework, particularly the timeline structures. The KIP was therefore changed to follow the consumer group record scheme more closely. Share groups now persist assignments and member epochs, which fixes the soft-state management problems and makes group membership reliable across coordinator restarts.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer gives the gold reasoning: survival of assignments across a coordinator change matters less, there is no need to transfer partitions safely between members, and persisting is unnecessary. It then adds that the decision was later reversed. That addition provides further context and does not contradict the gold reasoning.

Sophie Blee-Goldman added that a readable numeric scheme for versions is nearly impossible, and that commit IDs need to be strings.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer gives the gold answer's reason: Prometheus accepts only numeric metric values, and version strings such as 3.5.0 are not valid numbers. The extra details it adds do not contradict the gold answer.

questions.question: How does the way records reach the dead-letter topic under KIP-1191 (share groups) differ from KIP-1034 (Kafka Streams)?
questions.gold_answer: Share-group DLQs automatically copy unprocessable records to another topic, while KIP-1034 routes them through Streams exception handlers (withDeadLetterQueueRecord) that users can customize.

answer.text:
Under KIP-1191 (share groups), the broker writes the DLQ record. Records that are rejected or exceed their delivery limit are undeliverable, and the broker copies them onto the DLQ topic. The planned sequence is: the record moves to a new Archiving state, the DLQ record is written, then the state becomes Archived. The Archived state must not be written before the DLQ write, so a share coordinator failover can still ensure the DLQ write happens. Because the broker doesn't know why a record was DLQed, the exception-detail headers (__dlq.errors.exception.*) were removed from the KIP. Copying the original record payload is controlled by a group-level config. DLQ topics are not auto-created by default, though auto-creation with cluster defaults is an option. The DLQ topic name prefix is checked when the DLQ record is written. A metric counts failures to write to the DLQ.

Under KIP-1034 (Kafka Streams), the DLQ record is built and sent from the client side, inside the Streams application, by exception handlers. These handlers can be overridden to change how the DLQ record is built, for example to mask the payload or add headers. The record carries the raw key and value, the original headers and context headers, plus error headers with a common prefix (__streams.errors.*) that hold exception details such as class, message and stack trace. The value is null if the failure happens in a punctuate. Streams does not try to auto-create the DLQ topic, so it must be pre-created or auto-created by the broker. If a DLQ record cannot be sent, the exception goes to the uncaughtExceptionHandler. DLQ records are not meant to be reprocessed by the Streams application.

In short, KIP-1191 does broker-side copying of undeliverable records, driven by share-partition state, with limited error context. KIP-1034 does client-side, handler-driven production with rich exception metadata.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer covers both required facts. Share-group DLQs are broker-side automatic copying of undeliverable records. KIP-1034 routes records through Streams exception handlers that users can override. The answer doesn't name withDeadLetterQueueRecord, but the handler-based mechanism is clearly stated, and nothing contradicts the gold answer.

questions.question: In the KIP-1030 discussion, why was deriving the copier and expiration thread pool sizes from the original remote log thread pool setting considered incorrect?
questions.gold_answer: Followers' work (fetching highest-uploaded remote offset) is light, while leaders' copy and delete work is heavy; also it broke backward compatibility, e.g. 10 threads in 3.8 became 30 in 3.9.

answer.text:
Kamal Chandraprakash argued in the KIP-1030 discussion that deriving the copier and expiration pool sizes from `remote.log.manager.thread.pool.size` (the -1 default) was wrong for several reasons:

1. The original pool is now used differently. After KIP-950/KIP-956 split the pool, `remote.log.manager.thread.pool.size` is used by replicas to fetch the highest-uploaded remote offset for follower partitions. The copier pool is used by leaders to upload segments, and the expiration pool is used by leaders to delete expired segments.

2. The workloads differ. A broker is leader for some partitions and follower for others. Follower work is light-weight (only fetching the highest-uploaded remote offset), whereas leader work is heavy (copying and deleting segments). Sizing the leader pools from the follower-oriented setting therefore looks incorrect.

3. It broke backward compatibility. The -1 default was meant to preserve compatibility, but it did not. A user running 10 threads in v3.8 would get 30 threads in v3.9, because the original, copier and expiration pools would each get 10.

Because of this, he proposed changing the copier and expiration defaults from -1 to 10. He said this would also make validation smoother when those configs are made dynamic. In the later addendum, the follower pool default was proposed to drop to 2, since follower tasks are light-weight.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer gives both required reasons: follower work is light while leader copy and delete work is heavy, and backward compatibility broke, with 10 threads in 3.8 becoming 30 in 3.9. Nothing in it contradicts the gold answer.

questions.question: How does KIP-1157's purpose for custom KafkaPrincipalBuilder implementations differ from the purpose of KIP-982?
questions.gold_answer: KIP-1157 makes implementing KafkaPrincipalSerde mandatory alongside the builder, while KIP-982 gives custom builders access to SslPrincipalMapper and kerberosShortNamer.

answer.text: KIP-1157 and KIP-982 both concern custom KafkaPrincipalBuilder implementations, but they have different goals. KIP-1157 (Johnny Wang) is about enforcement. It requires that a KafkaPrincipalSerde implementation be provided alongside KafkaPrincipalBuilder, a requirement that was previously only noted in the interface comments. Reviewers pointed out that this could break backward compatibility, since builders that implement only KafkaPrincipalBuilder would no longer compile. It would also affect DefaultKafkaPrincipalBuilder, which currently extends both interfaces. KIP-982 (Raghu B) is about enhancement. It gives custom KafkaPrincipalBuilder implementations access to SslPrincipalMapper and KerberosShortNamer, so they can parse mapping rules such as SSL_PRINCIPAL_MAPPING_RULES_CONFIG from BrokerSecurityConfigs. This improves flexibility and usability. In short, KIP-1157 tightens the contract by making the Serde mandatory, while KIP-982 extends what custom builders can do by exposing the principal mapper and Kerberos short namer.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer gives both required facts. KIP-1157 makes a KafkaPrincipalSerde implementation mandatory alongside the builder. KIP-982 gives custom builders access to SslPrincipalMapper and the Kerberos short namer. Nothing in it contradicts the gold answer.

questions.question: How does the scope of KIP-1202 on broker and controller listener alignment differ from KIP-1060 on controller advertised listeners?
questions.gold_answer: KIP-1060 proposes allowing advertised.listeners on KRaft controllers, where it was forbidden. KIP-1202 aligns broker and controller advertised.listeners behaviour when listeners uses the 0.0.0.0 wildcard address.

answer.text:
KIP-1060 (Gantigmaa Selenge, June 2024) was about exposing/allowing advertised.listeners for KRaft controllers, which was previously forbidden. It was later discarded because José Armando García Sancio was already implementing the capability as part of the KIP-853 implementation (PR 16235). Selenge then raised a PR to document that users can configure advertised.listeners for controllers, and José created KAFKA-17048 to document the changes and recommended configuration for new clusters.

KIP-1202 (Jiunn-Yang, Sept 2025) is narrower and comes after controllers could already use advertised.listeners. It aligns the broker and controller behaviour of advertised.listeners and listeners, specifically when listeners is set to the special value 0.0.0.0 (e.g. PLAINTEXT://0.0.0.0:9092). In that case, if advertised.listeners is null, an IllegalArgumentException is thrown saying it cannot use the non-routable meta-address 0.0.0.0. KIP-1202 also addresses an inconsistency in the null/empty handling: null is valid for both broker and controller, while empty is valid only for the controller (the broker errors on an empty value). Chia-Ping Tsai noted the controller should also reject an empty value, and Jiunn-Yang agreed to disallow an empty list.

In short, KIP-1060 was about enabling advertised.listeners on controllers at all, while KIP-1202 is about making the broker and controller behave consistently regarding the 0.0.0.0 listener and null/empty validation. The sources do not give KIP-1202's full details beyond these points.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer covers both required facts. It says KIP-1060 allows advertised.listeners on KRaft controllers, where it was previously forbidden. It says KIP-1202 aligns broker and controller advertised.listeners behaviour when listeners uses 0.0.0.0. The extra details it adds do not contradict the gold answer.

questions.question: Do KIP-1092's option for leaving the group on close and KIP-1153's fluent refactor of CloseOptions target the same client API?
questions.gold_answer: No. KIP-1092 extends Consumer#close, while KIP-1153 refactors Kafka Streams CloseOptions.

answer.text: No. KIP-1092 extends the Consumer API: it adds a new CloseOptions class so that Consumer#close(CloseOptions) can choose whether the consumer leaves the group. KIP-1153 targets the Kafka Streams API instead. It refactors the existing KafkaStreams.CloseOptions, which has a public constructor, into a fluent style. The plan is to deprecate the nested class and create a new top-level Streams CloseOptions. The two are related, since KIP-1153 follows the KIP-1092 pattern (static entry methods, `with` setters, possibly an enum for leave-group). Even so, the participants agreed to keep two separate CloseOptions classes, because Streams and the consumer have different default behavior and may diverge later.

questions.question: How does the approach of KIP-1200 toward ClientQuotaCallback's cluster-metadata update method differ from that of KIP-1162?
questions.gold_answer: KIP-1162 proposes redesigning ClientQuotaCallback#updateClusterMetadata, while KIP-1200 proposes deprecating that same method.

answer.text: KIP-1162 tried to redesign ClientQuotaCallback#updateClusterMetadata, while KIP-1200 proposes to deprecate it and introduce no replacement. KIP-1162 would replace the heavy, partly outdated Cluster object with a lighter, more efficient interface for the metadata passed to the method. It would add a new updateClusterMetadata overload (taking a ClusterMetadata) and a new interface, with the old method deprecated, so that users could migrate. That meant many new public APIs. KIP-1200 takes the opposite route. Kuan-Po Tseng and Chia-Ping Tsai argued that the method is error-prone (see KAFKA-19122). It was not implemented in KRaft for over three years until it was reintroduced in 4.0, with no reported issues in that time, and it is "almost" unused. Fixing it properly would need significant effort and many public interfaces wrapping images, because Cluster is heavy. So KIP-1200 deprecates the method, with removal planned for 5.0, and offers no alternative method. Kuan-Po said he considers KIP-1162 dropped now that KIP-1200 is being voted on. Mickael Maison objected that the two KIPs contradict each other. He also said he knows of multiple ClientQuotaCallback implementations that rely on the method, and he did not want to vote for deprecation without a clear plan for users. Chia-Ping said that if users do need the method, KIP-1162 could be revisited.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer states the required contrast: KIP-1162 redesigns ClientQuotaCallback#updateClusterMetadata and KIP-1200 deprecates it. The additional detail does not contradict the gold answer.

questions.question: Do KIP-1161 and KIP-1202 address the same configuration behavior?
questions.gold_answer: No. KIP-1161 covers null/empty-list validation for list configs such as early.start.listeners, log.dirs and plugin.path, while KIP-1202 covers advertised.listeners behavior when listeners is set to 0.0.0.0.

answer.text: No, they overlap only partly. KIP-1161 ("cleanup.policy shouldn't be empty") is the broader KIP. It covers empty and duplicate values in LIST-type configs, including cleanup.policy, controller.listener.names, and several security and filter configs. KIP-1202 is narrower. It aligns broker and controller behavior for advertised.listeners and listeners, especially when listeners is set to 0.0.0.0 (PLAINTEXT://0.0.0.0:9092) and advertised.listeners is null, which throws an IllegalArgumentException. The two touch advertised.listeners from different angles. KIP-1161 changed its type from string to list, and Chia-Ping said that if KIP-1161 addresses this config, the controller should also reject an empty value. Jun and Jiunn-Yang agreed to leave the validator and the 0.0.0.0 issue to KIP-1202. Chia-Ping also described the broker/controller inconsistency (null valid for both, empty valid only for the controller) as something KIP-1202 will address. So the two are related and share advertised.listeners, but they do not address the same behavior overall.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer gets the overall 'no' right and correctly says KIP-1202 handles advertised.listeners when listeners is 0.0.0.0. For KIP-1161 it describes empty/duplicate validation of LIST-type configs, which broadly matches the gold. However, it names cleanup.policy and controller.listener.names rather than the gold's examples (early.start.listeners, log.dirs, plugin.path), and it never mentions null validation. It also hedges with 'overlap only partly'. The core contrast is preserved without contradiction, but the specific facts are incomplete.

questions.question: How does KIP-1248's approach to serving historical tiered-storage data differ from KIP-1255's?
questions.gold_answer: KIP-1248 lets consumer clients fetch directly from remote tiered storage, bypassing brokers, while KIP-1255 adds a lightweight broker role (Remote Read Replica) that serves historical reads from remote storage.

answer.text:
KIP-1248 (with its consumer-side sub-KIP-1254) lets the consumer read tiered data directly from remote storage, bypassing the broker for the bulk data. The broker's FetchResponse redirects the consumer, giving it the remote segment location and byte-position hints from the OffsetIndex. The consumer then uses a new plugin (RemoteStorageFetcher, earlier called RemoteStorageReader) to pull byte ranges straight from S3/GCS/Azure and parses the segment format itself. Consumers must opt in (fetch.remote.enabled), and the design falls back to a normal broker fetch on timeout, connection or auth failure, a missing plugin, or a storage-format version mismatch. Kamal Chandraprakash noted the costs of this approach: non-Java clients must reimplement the logic, the client becomes heavier with remote-storage dependencies, and it may not be compatible with all client APIs.

KIP-1255 (Remote Read Replicas) keeps clients unchanged and instead introduces a lightweight broker role dedicated to serving historical reads from remote storage. Per Kamal's description, these brokers need little disk or memory, can sit in the same AZ as consumers, serve only FETCH requests from remote storage, and can be scaled quickly, similar to reading from a preferred replica. The sources describe KIP-1255 only briefly, and it was in draft stage. So the main difference is where the remote read happens: in the consumer for KIP-1248/1254, and in a dedicated broker for KIP-1255.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer states that KIP-1248 has consumers fetch directly from remote storage, bypassing brokers, and that KIP-1255 introduces a lightweight broker role (Remote Read Replicas) serving historical reads from remote storage. Both required facts are present and nothing contradicts the gold answer.

questions.question: In the KIP-910 discussion on updating source offsets without producing records, why did Sagar choose to implement the offset-only mechanism through special records passed through the existing write path?
questions.gold_answer: Once the connector emits SourceRecords, the framework already writes them to a topic and commits offsets, so it was the least invasive change at the framework level.

answer.text: In the April 2023 design, Sagar produced "heartbeat records" to emit offsets without new records. He said the reason was that once the framework gets SourceRecords, the rest of the code is already in place to write them to a topic and commit offsets. He considered that the least invasive option in terms of framework-level changes. He also said the main purpose of the heartbeat records was to emit offsets without any new records, which addresses the primary concern of offsets stalling. He acknowledged that a framework-only heartbeat approach later on could cause naming confusion. The KIP was later revised to a newer approach that dropped the explicit topic, so this rationale applies to the earlier draft.

questions.judge_rationale: The system answer gives both required points: once the framework receives SourceRecords, the existing code already writes them to a topic and commits offsets, and this made it the least invasive change at the framework level. The extra detail does not contradict the gold answer.
